title: Pedestrians appear unable to leave sidewalks, rendering pedestrian routing in cities poorly supported
body:
In OpenStreetMap data, sidewalks are typically drawn separate from the road, even if there is no kerb in between. Thus, when routing, there is no physical connection to the road and walkers are routed all the way around any physical connection.
The concept of 'crossing a road', leaving a sidewalk, does not exist. That makes pedestrian routing in a city with many sidewalks poorly supported and comes with odd detours.
Google Maps appears not to draw sidewalks as such, avoiding the issue. But once they are properly drawn, then routing software should understand how walkers walk on them and how road crossings work.

See screenshot for a typical example. The footpath is adjacent to the local road, as usual. If there are no sideways at the same side of the road, the detour can be infinite. Just as long as it takes to have that physical (in OSM terms) connection.
